title: Australian parents rebel against restrictive lunchbox policies, new University of Adelaide study finds
text:
7NEWS brings you the latest local news from Australia and around the world. Stay up to date with all of the breaking sport, politics, entertainment, finance, weather and business headlines. Today's news, live updates & all the latest breaking stories from 7NEWS.
Australian parents are pushing back against strict school lunch box policies, claiming the rules are now so strict they’re in a constant battle to make sure their kids don’t go hungry. New research from the University of Adelaide has shed a light on the daily pressure families face trying to pack meals that are healthy, allergy-safe, eco-friendly and able to be eaten in under 10 minutes.
The study, conducted with 16 South Australian families, found most parents are prioritising food their children will actually eat over school-imposed rules. “While parents aim to provide nutritious meals, concerns about whether children will eat the food often take precedence,” researchers said. Time constraints, tight budgets and convenience are driving many to rely on prepackaged snacks, despite schools pushing for fresh, unpackaged “nude food”. Brisbane father-of-two, Jarred Crafter said schools are becoming the new “Almond mums” — a term used to describe parents overly obsessed with healthy eating. “Kids should be able to eat a balanced diet without being obsessed about it being healthy or not,” he told 7NEWS.com.au. Eco-friendly policies are also proving difficult for parents, the study found. While most support the idea, many parents said in the research it was not practical during the morning rush. “This is a whole different ball game to how we grew up,” Adelaide mother-of-three Isabell Cummins said. “We grew up with a meat sandwich sitting outside in our bags, a doughnut, a packet of chips and maybe some fruit with a dip and we shared our food around, it was like a swap meet. “If you hated your ham sandwich, you could easily find someone who wanted to trade it for their Vegemite and cheese. “Now, I’ve been given notes from the school if the dip I send with my children’s cut-up fruit is unhealthy. “My kids play a lot of sport, they need carbs and protein, but if I send them to school with a pasta dish too many times, or a few chocolate protein balls after a big weekend, I’d get a note.“ Banning nuts — due to the rise in anaphylaxis among children — had also led to parents needing to pivot. “I’m fine with nut-free, but if I had to do dairy or egg free, I’d struggle find something that not only will keep my kids happy with a full stomach, but juggle their own diet needs,” Cummins said “There’s nothing worse for both teachers and kids than hungry tummies.” Nutrition Australia is offering support through its National Lunchbox Week campaign, encouraging parents to pack balanced meals with grains, dairy, protein, fruit and vegetables. Their top tip — Bento-style lunch boxes — which can be ideal for picky eaters who prefer their food to be separated. The organisation also recommends a simple lunch such as a sandwich or wrap, fruit or vegetable, a snack like yogurt or popcorn, and water.
